MR. CAOUETTE  STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING PENSION PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I regret that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) is not in his seat. My question of privilege arises out of a question I directed to him last Thursday, April 23, as reported at page 2487 of Hansard, which reads as follows:
Can the Prime Minister tell us whether the agreement reached between Ottawa and Quebec respecting the Canada pension plan contains a provision allowing a province to change the contributions or the benefits without obtaining beforehand the consent of Ottawa and the other provinces?
To which the Prime Minister answered the following:
The agreement is that there will be a universal pension scheme the provisions of which will be applicable to all Canadians.
At that time we accepted the Prime Minister's answer, but yesterday the Quebec premier stated in explicit, clear and precise terms, and I quote:
I stated, said Mr. Lesage, and repeated and I repeat again that there will be a provincial pension plan in Quebec, a strictly provincial plan. The contributions will be collected by the province. They will be administered by the province. The benefits will be paid out by the province or by a provincial commission. One hundred per cent of the investments will be made by the province according to decisions made by the province. Provincial legislation will be introduced on that matter.
For the information of parliament, will the Prime Minister say whether he was aware of that matter or not? Because we were certainly misled. It clearly appears that Quebec will be given a double pension plan: one provincial and one national, according to statements by the premier and the Prime Minister. I should like the house to be informed on that matter.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harry W. Hays (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUPPORT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a statement on the new dairy policy for the production year opening May 1.
I think the basic goal of all agricultural policies should be to maintain and improve the position of Canadian farmers in the national economy and to promote efficiency of production. This is the principle on which we are building our policy on all stabilization prices for farm products, including the dairy products concerned in the statement I am now making. We believe that efficient stabilization levels should ensure farmers a sound and stable return, consistent with realistic economics; keep Canadian farm products competitive both in price and quality, on the home market as well as in the markets of the world; and provide Canadian consumers with the highest quality food at the most reasonable prices possible.
A year ago I announced certain changes in the dairy support policy designed to pursue this general goal. For dairy products specifically, the changes were designed to bring consumption and production into better balance and at the same time to divert certain quantities of milk to the production of cheddar cheese.
I am pleased to be able to report that this program has over the past year been successful in meeting these objectives. For the dairy year now ending, total domestic consumption and export of dairy products are essentially in balance with production. Estimated butter production for the dairy year ending tomorrow is 352.1 million pounds. Estimated domestic consumption for the year was 357.4 million

Dairy Support Policy
pounds. Thus domestic consumption will exceed production by approximately five million pounds.
In addition to this we have made substantial export sales of butter in the form of butter oil, leaving estimated total butter stocks, including trade holdings, at the end of the dairy year of approximately 165 million pounds. This compares with total stocks a year ago of 203 million pounds. At the same time returns to producers of milk for manufacturing purposes have been above those of the previous year, while costs to the federal treasury, other than those associated with the accrued surplus, have been down.
Meanwhile milk production has remained strong and production of Cheddar cheese has risen. Production of Cheddar cheese for the dairy year now closing is an estimated 134.1 million pounds, an increase of 14 per cent over that of the previous year of 118.4 million pounds. Cheddar consumption was maintained at almost the same level, at 100 million pounds for this year compared to 102 million pounds for the previous year. Exports of Cheddar were higher this year by 14 per cent than for the previous year, at 31.2 million pounds compared to 27.4 million pounds. Cheddar stocks for the year are estimated at 46 million pounds compared to 37 million pounds a year ago.
In line with the action taken a year ago, changes in the dairy support program for the new year opening May 1 will be toward a further rationalization of the program. We are trying to put an emphasis on quality production while at the same time maintaining the basic support levels currently protecting the producer.
In order to narrow the gap between the support level and the selling price of the agricultural stabilization board, the board's price for butter will be set at 53 cents per pound for 40 score creamery butter, basis Montreal and Toronto. This is a reduction in the consumer subsidy of 1 cent per pound. It will transfer a slight proportion of the dairy subsidy cost from taxpayers as a whole to the actual users of butter. The change is not expected to have any effect on butter consumption and will mean a saving to the taxpayers of an estimated $3.5 million. Meanwhile the support level for producers will be maintained at 64 cents a pound by the board. This means manufacturers will be authorized to pay eligible producers 13.3 cents per pound of butterfat used for production of creamery butter.
The support for cheddar cheese will be maintained at the existing level of 32J cents per pound, but the basis on which it is paid will be revised to stress production of high quality cheese. Instead of paying 30 cents 
per hundredweight on milk used for cheddar cheese production, a payment of 3.6 cents per pound will be made on Canada first grade cheddar made from milk supplied by eligible producers. This will permit manufacturers of such cheese to pay at least the equivalent of the 30 cents per hundredweight assistance for cheese milk during the year now ending. The purchase program on dry skim milk and the assistance on milk used for the manufacture of casein will be reinstated on the same basis as in effect during the 196364 production year. Export assistance on certain dairy products will continue in the coming dairy year with the products and levels being made known to the trade by the board in due course.
In making this announcement I would stress that these moves represent another step toward solving what has been one of the most difficult agricultural problems facing not only Canada but many other countries in the world.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUPPORT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we welcome the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture in the house today in regard to dairy policy. The dairy industry are accustomed to having this statement made prior to May 1, the beginning of the dairy year, and in this instance we are glad that the minister, although leaving it to the last moment, has made this statement. We are very pleased indeed to learn that one of the major dairy problems is being brought to a close, in that we find in the announcement made by the minister today that the domestic consumption and export of butter are being brought into line with the production of this commodity. This will alleviate one of the major problems of the dairy industry.
We welcome the statement made by the minister that he is going to continue the support on cheddar cheese, that butter will be subsidized and emphasis will be placed on the production of first grade cheddar cheese. We will have to wait until we can consider this report in some detail in order to deal specifically with the different parts of the announcement that has been made today but we are certainly pleased, sir, that the minister has taken this opportunity to announce to the country the dairy policy of this government.

Is there an agreement in effect between the government of Canada and the government of India which restricts to 300 the number of citizens of India who may come to Canada in any one year for permanent residence and, if so. will steps be taken to rescind this agreement?

In 1951 the Canadian and Indian governments entered into an agreement providing for the annual admission to Canada of 150 citizens of India over and above those categories of persons who were already eligible for admission under then existing immigration regulations. The agreement was revised in 1957 to increase the number involved from 150 to 300.
On the surface it might appear that this agreement is restrictive in nature as is suggested by the wording of the hon. member's question. However, it must be borne in mind that the agreement was concluded at a time when immigration regulations were not as broad in scope as they are at present. In effect therefore the agreement took the form of an extension of the admissible categories for citizens of India.
With the coming into force of new immigration regulations in February 1962, which gave everyone an equal opportunity to qualify for admission in his or her own right, the need for the agreement from the viewpoint of the Canadian government ceased. Discussions have since been held between representatives of the Canadian and Indian governments with a view to cancelling the agreement. In the meantime the agreement has remained in effect.
I would also like to say that the hon. member, in putting his question, has given me the opportunity to qualify to some extent the observations I made previously on this subject at page 1469 of Hansard during the course of the debate on ihe immigration supplementary estimates on March 25, 1964.

1.	Is it the intention to establish a new dominion observatory in western Canada, and especially in either the provinces of Alberta or British Columbia and, if so, has a decision been reached as to a specific locality?
2.	What are the essential conditions which go to determine a suitable location?
3.	What would be the estimated cost of constructing such an observatory, and how long would it take?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
1. The Department of Mines and Technical Surveys is presently studying a proposal put forward by the dominion observatory to build a large optical telescope of at least 150 inches in diameter, in that region of the country best suited to astronomical observations. If constructed, it is planned that this new equipment would be available on equitable terms to astronomers from every province of Canada. The specific site of the proposed telescope has not yet been chosen. However, the requirement for high altitude has limited the search to the mountainous regions of the country and more particularly to the southern parts of British Columbia and Alberta.
2. The site of a large optical telescope must be high enough to be above local dust and disturbed air (usually 6,000 to 7,000 feet). It must be in a region not subject to rapidly moving weather fronts, to great extremes of temperature, and to much auroral activity, and it must be well away from industrial development and large population centres. Low rainfall and clear skies are essential as

well as steady and transparent air. These factors, however, serve only to limit the search and final selection must be made on the basis of optical tests.
3.	The capital cost of such an observatory is estimated to be $9,671,000 spread over a period of six to seven years.

Is a re-examination of Canada's grain-grading system being made with a view to bringing it into line with grain grading procedures in other countries and, if so, when is it likely that such a revised grain grading method will be introduced?

Inasmuch as Canada's grain grading system is acknowledged to be superior there is no consideration being given to bringing it into line with grading procedures in other countries. However, with the rapidly changing technology in the baking industry in consuming countries, which require somewhat different qualities in the grain that goes into the end product than heretofore, it is felt that a careful and thorough examination of all that is involved in grading grain, particularly wheat, is desirable. Consideration is at present being given to undertaking such a study.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to raise a question of privilege which I believe affects all members of the house. Appearing on the order paper today is question No. 826, addressed to the Minister of Labour, which reads in part as follows:
1. Up to the present date, how many workers over the age of 45 have been placed in employment in Canada through the offices of the national employment service as a result of the program by which their salaries are supplemented to the maximum of $75 per month out of public funds?
Appearing in the press of this country yesterday under the byline of the Canadian Press is a release in the name of the Minister of Labour, and I will read it in part:
Labour minister MacEachen announced Monday-
That is the day before yesterday.
-that 2,347 job openings were approved under the incentive program whereby the federal government pays a special subsidy to employers hiring and training workers 45 years and older. But by the March 31 deadline for hiring older workers, only 1,811 workers had been put in approved jobs.
Mr. Speaker, the way members have of obtaining information in this house is by means of the order paper. Many of us try assiduously to follow the rules of the house, and in an effort to do so I placed my question on the order paper on April 21. It was there on Monday last. The minister chose to give this information to the press of the country instead of answering the question in the House of Commons. I submit this is a breach of the rules of the house, it is contempt of parliament and in fact it is government by press release.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ALLEGED INACCU- RATE STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. On April 24 the Associate Minister of National Defence, in reply to a supplementary question posed by me which appears on pages 2539 and 2540 of Hansard, stated that his department was doing everything it could to phase out operations at the Point Edward naval base as slowly as possible. He continued by stating:
A ship which was not scheduled to go into the Point Edward naval base has now been directed to
Inquiries of the Ministry
go there in order to be refitted, so that work will be provided for a longer period and we will then be able to phase out more slowly the work at Point Edward naval base.
It has only now come to my attention that the naval vessel to which I presume he referred, H.M.C.S. Swansea, is not at the Point Edward naval base but is at a private shipyard at Sydney where only five employees from the base are employed at the moment. The result of the minister's statement, which was accepted by all the news media in the area to mean that a new refit job was available for this base, has been to promote false hopes and disappointment in the minds of the employees who are already tormented by the fact they are to be without employment in the very near future.
I am not suggesting that the minister deliberately misled the house, the employees and others in the area concerned. However, it is my hope that the hon. gentleman will now correct his grievous error and see that a naval vessel is allocated to this base so the phasing out will be slowed down as he promised, since this government appears to be quite adamant in its stand that this base must close.

subtopic: ALLEGED INACCU- RATE STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext: I have not had an opportunity of seeing the article to which the hon. member referred. What I said the other day was that in order to extend the work, to phase out the work at Point Edward more slowly, the government had decided to send a ship to the Point Edward naval base which had not been scheduled for that base. I shall be glad to look into this particular matter. I can tell the house that there was certainly no intention to mislead the house. It is a fact that a ship was sent to the Point Edward naval base for repairs that was not scheduled to go there.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Now that General Gyani has spoken along the line of questions asked by the opposition, namely that the situation in certain parts of Cyprus is such that it raises serious implications concerning the role of the United Nations force, I ask the minister- we have to get this information from the press, I would point out-whether any action has been taken to do that which we have suggested, that is to give reasonable powers to the United Nations force; particularly because of an Associated Press dispatch which indicates that all the Canadian troops in Cyprus have to do is observe developments and report back to United Nations headquarters or intervene to protect the civilian population if necessary. Is the minister now in a position to give this house more complete and concise information than he has given up to the present time?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman said I gave something to the press which I had not given to the house.
No, he did not.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Well, I misunderstood the hon. gentleman. If he had said that I was going to correct it. General Gyani issued a subsequent statement to that already referred to by my hon. friend. At the conclusion of that statement General Gyani said, and I quote:
It Is my firm belief now that peaceful conditions can be restored and maintained in Cyprus, and we in the United Nations peace force will work relentlessly to bring about active measures to reduce tension and eliminate fear and assist in every way possible toward achieving quiet and peace in the island.
Since the interrogation in this house yesterday there has been a subsiding of incidents in Cyprus. In addition, the secretary general, who is now in Paris conferring on the matter,


has issued a statement and a report to the security council suggesting what course should be taken by the United Nations force in the light of the situation that developed over the week end. I had hoped that we would have the full text of this statement so I could table it in the house today. I expect it will be circulated in the United Nations some time this afternoon. I may say that this statement is partly in response to a conversation I had on Friday last-I know this does not please the right hon. gentleman-
No, it is ridiculous.

I know it does not please the right hon. gentleman, but the fact is that it is partly in response to a conversation I had with the secretary general last Friday night, conversations which the secretary general has had with certain contributing countries' representatives, as well as talks with representatives of the United Nations, the United States , and other countries. When the text of the secretary general's report is available it will be tabled forthwith. As a matter of fact, I believe with the permission of the house, I should table the statement of General Gyani, dated late yesterday.
Does the house give consent to the tabling of this statement?
Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, I ask the hon. gentleman this question. Has he made representations to the effect that the role of the United Nations force, and I refer particularly to the Canadians, shall not be that of simply a passive policeman but that the force shall undertake remedial and effective action which in their opinion is necessary?

I have already answered that question twice, yesterday and partly today. I indicated that on Friday last when I saw the secretary general, I told him that in the light of the situation as it was reported to us by our high commissioner in Cyprus, and as reported from other sources, it would seem that the United Nations force was being placed in a difficult position. The secretary general acknowledged this. Because I am concerned about the operations of that force, I am precluded from going any further.
Now, I can say that the secretary general has made a statement in Paris today. His statement is preliminary to a report which he is circulating to the members of the United Nations security council, and that report will be available some time today. I ask my hon. friend to consider his question in the light of that report.

I have considered the question in the light of the uncertain reports

the hon. gentleman has given this house on all occasions. I will be glad, however, to wait until we receive an authentic statement from General Gyani.

I do not want to quarrel with my hon. friend, but I do know something about the delicacy of this situation. It is not fair to our soldiers; it is not fair to the United Nations; it is not fair to the Canadian people, to say-
Oh, oh.

-that I have given
uncertain reports. I have given reports that were exact and precise. They have to do with a very difficult situation, and I may say to my right hon. friend, the reaction I get-* and I have my appreciation of what reactions can be-is that the right hon. gentleman would do himself more credit by helping the government in a situation such as this.
Hear, hear.
Mr. Speaker, that last observation deserves an answer, and I simply say to the hon. gentleman that what he has said is bluff, and pompous bluff at that.

Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The latest report to come over the wires indicates that the British ambassador has been instructed to interview the secretary general of the United Nations regarding the inactivity of the United Nations force in Cyprus, and I want to ask the minister two questions to save the trouble of getting up on a supplementary.
First, are similar representations being made by the Canadian government to the secretary general of the United Nations? Second, does the Canadian government share the view that the presence of the United Nations force in Cyprus has effectively deprived the Turkish Cypriots of any outside aid, and therefore it is the responsibility of the United Nations force to provide sufficient protection for Turkish Cypriots?

Mr. Speaker, with regard to the first part of the question, the Canadian ambassador saw the secretary general of the United Nations twice on Saturday, and he was in touch three times yesterday with Mr. Ralph Bunche, who was acting in the absence of the secretary general. In addition, he conferred with Mr. Adlai Stevenson on Saturday and again yesterday.
I may say that the United States undersecretary of state for foreign affairs is in Ottawa, and I conferred with him on this matter this morning. I have also been in touch 20220-173
Inquiries of the Ministry with the foreign office in the United Kingdom. I am sure that the actions of the United Nations force in Cyprus, notwithstanding the difficulties, have had a preventive effect. I hope this effect will continue, particularly in the light of the report which we are awaiting from the secretary general.

The minister may have overlooked the second part of my question in which I asked whether the government shared the view that, since the presence of the United Nations force in Cyprus has effectively deprived the Turkish Cypriots of any outside aid, it is the responsibility of the United Nations to provide protection for Turkish Cypriots. Is this view being pressed upon the secretary general of the United Nations?
May I also remind him that yesterday he said Canadian troops were not directly involved in negotiations in the Kyrenia pass, yet a report came in this morning that it was Canadian troops who transmitted the request for the Turkish forces to withdraw, and the rejection was transmitted through the Canadian troops to the Cypriot forces.

Mr. Speaker, all I can properly do is to indicate that the Canadian government, maintaining a neutral position as a member of the United Nations force, has made representations, through its representative to the United Nations and its high commissioner in Cyprus, along the lines suggested by the hon. gentleman. Those representations were perfectly compatible with the desirable neutral position we must maintain.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a supplementary question to the Associate Minister of National Defence, and I may say it is also supplementary to a starred question he answered for me on Monday. Does he consider it fair to provide special allowances to our troops in Cyprus which are not equal to the allowances paid to our troops in the Congo and other overseas areas where they are serving?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Cardin (Associate Minister of Nalional Defence):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is not my impression that our troops in Cyprus are getting less than our troops in the Congo or anywhere else.

Mr. Speaker, I addressed a question to the Associate Minister of National Defence asking him about the special allowances which were made available in Cyprus as compared with those paid to troops in the Congo, New Guinea

Inquiries of the Ministry and other areas of the world. The associate minister told me there was no difference in the special allowances made available.
However, in the answer he provided to me as reported on page 2590 of Hansard he referred me to the public accounts of Canada, March 31, 1963, section 20, pages 23-25. From this I find that the special allowance for those in the Congo is $100 per month and that for troops in New Guinea it is $90 a month. When I look at the answer the hon. gentleman gave me with regard to the troops in Cyprus I see that the special allowance amounts to $69 a month.
I am pretty mixed up now. Either the minister has given me incorrect information today or he gave me incorrect information on Monday. He certainly gave me incorrect information at some time; and I should like to have the matter cleared up.

Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member knows the correct information was that given in the return. I apologize to the hon. member for having led him astray in this sense, that I led him to understand there was no difference in the amount of allowances that was paid. I have subsequently been informed that the special allowance for people serving in the Congo is $100 and the reason for this additional amount of money paid to the people in the Congo is, of course, the difficulty of serving in that very hot country.

Could I ask a question supplementary, Mr. Speaker, to my other question. I ask the minister, will he give consideration to increasing the amount of the special allowance for troops serving in Cyprus, in view of the great risk they are undertaking at the present time?
That matter will be considered, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Chairman, as was mentioned in the budget speech only about a score of tariff changes are proposed by these resolutions. About half of these, indeed somewhat more than half, stem from two tariff board reports which the government received in 1962 and 1963. These tariff board reports related to oilfield equipment and to certain glassware and chinaware for decorating, respectively. They recommended changes in tariff items which were bound by the general agreement on tariffs and trade; hence they could not be implemented until the former GATT commitments were renegotiated. This has now been done.
The effect of the first two of the four resolutions now before the committee is to implement the results of these negotiations. The third resolution provides for a miscellaneous group of amendments. Most of them are of a relieving nature, and the purpose of the others is merely to clarify or modernize existing provisions. The fourth resolution is the usual coming into force provision. It follows the traditional practice of bringing all tariff changes provisionally into effect on the day following the budget, conditional of course on their subsequently being approved by parliament.

Before resuming my seat, possibly I should say a few words relating specifically to resolution 1. As I mentioned, it represents a negotiated package stemming from two tariff board reports. However, it involves four items which did not appear in these reports. One of these is a bound item which it was desired to reword for purposes of clarification, and which was included in the negotiations as a matter of convenience. The other three items represent what I believe GATT technicians refer to as "outside compensation". By way of explanation I should point out that while the tariff board report on oilfield equipment recommended some increases and some reductions in bound rates of duty, the increases somewhat overbalanced the reductions. Accordingly, in order to renegotiate our obligations in accordance with the GATT rules, it was necessary for us to make corresponding reductions in the rates on some other items. The concessions which were agreed upon in this connection as acceptable to both ourselves and our trading partners, and which are implemented by resolution 1, affect barytes, montan wax and bread. I am sure this change will be welcomed by most of them.
However, I noticed that the reduction is also made, although not so great, where the article is of a class or kind made in Canada. This leaves a very small margin of protection for the local manufacturer. I think when you consider the small margin of protection, plus the expense that is involved in trying to determine whether an article is of a class or kind made in Canada, we will realize the local manufacturer has little or no protection here.
I may cite as an example the first item mentioned, bolted steel tanks and parts thereof. Steel tanks for the oil well industry are made up in all sorts of sizes, shapes and capacities, from relatively small ones servicing one well to some of the giant tanks which are used at the start of the trans-Canada pipe line. We can easily see that a local manufacturer who makes one specific type of tank or tank plates and has a competitor who sells a tank which is slightly larger or slightly smaller in size or a different shape, finds that it is a moot point whether or not this is of a class or kind made in Canada. I suggest that the rough and ready rule in determining the question is whether or not the article can be used for substantially the same purpose by the same people. I can see that many people are going to be upset by the decisions made in connection with this item because we can carry that same sort of argument to pumps such as chemical injection pumps. A pump can be used for chemical injection purposes and it can also be used for another purpose. It is difficult to make these distinctions.

I know there is always going to be difficulty in making these decisions. I am not quarrelling with the honesty of the officials who have to make the decisions. These decisions are difficult, no matter how skilled they are or how much they know about industry. It is for that reason I am questioning the very minor amount of protection that is left in connection with this item, where an article is of a type made in Canada. Where you have a very small amount of protection and you have no margin for error or confusion as to whether or not a person is entitled to the protection, it is going to make people discouraged. They will not invest their money in Canadian enterprise in those areas in which it would be most helpful to the oil industry.
I am sure that the question of the convenience to the oil industry is perhaps not sufficiently impressed on the minds of the officials concerned. In so far as oil production, exploration or the installation of these tank farms is concerned, usually the contractor has a contract in which a time limit is set. He has to deal with a highly technical crew, and the question of how quickly they can complete the installation becomes very important, not just from the point of view of keeping the contract but from the point of view of cost involved. The question of a slight difference in cost must always be weighed against the question of convenience, that is of having the article there. If there is any shadow of doubt about an article the contractor will import what he calls the exact one, even if the Canadian article might do, despite this 5 per cent or 10 per cent tariff, because the amount of money is negligible when compared with the time saved and the certainty the correct article will be available.
I suggest that this is a rather shortsighted approach by the government, because it is worth more than that 5 per cent to the oil industry to give encouragement to Canadian manufacturers to invest their money in building a product in localities such as my area, where it is most wanted. It is always advantageous to the user of these supplies to have the local manufacturer right at hand, where there is not a problem of quick re-establishment of supplies and quick expansion in case of demand, where he can get them quickly and where he is in direct communication with the manufacturer to speed up his production.
The manufacturer is right in the field. He knows what the demand is and what demand may be coming. He can adjust his production very quickly to meet the demand and, not only that, he can vary his product to meet more exactly the requirements and specifications of the purchaser. Our suppliers are going to be very happy with the new field, but when they are going to invest their money-and I am thinking in terms of the establishment of industry in my riding and the well being of those established, especially the Canadian manufacturers-they have to look at the long term picture and view it from the standpoint of steady supply and production.
The conditions have changed. The steel plant in Edmonton has made an expansion and there will be more steel available than there was previously. There have been some new manufactures established on a rather small scale in my area, and I am sure the prospect of another large, new oil field, together with the known number of them, is the sort of solid indicator that Canadian manufacturers are looking for. That is why I was asking the parliamentary secretary particularly if there were any late representations-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: None.
-from production people, and what are the late representations from Canadian manufacturers on these tariffs involved in item 492.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I should point out that the report of the tariff board on reference No. 130 was tabled on October 7, 1963, and there were over three pages of companies which made representations to the board. The tariff board report, along with its recommendations which are contained in this resolution, has been available since October 1963, and as I understand it from officials of the department there have been no complaints. Nor have there been any complaints since the resolution itself was put on the order paper and became public knowledge, which usually occurs when people have a complaint. When a resolution appears on the order paper at the time of the budget speech, usually if people are terribly upset about it they will make complaints to the Minister of Finance, but that did not happen in this case.

Now to deal with the other question, there may have been changes in conditions. Of course one can assume there have been changes in conditions over the period during which the tariff board had been studying this. But the people who were aware of these changes, and who have made decisions since October 1963, have made those decisions with the full knowledge of what the tariff board was recommending in this regard. It is also very unlikely that the point of profit or loss, if one is building a new steel plant, for example, is going to be materially affected by the difference between a 5 per cent and a 10 per cent tariff on this item. Mind you, it will affect it, but I do not think a 10 per cent tariff protection would be a great tariff behind which to build an industry.
I would not want to quibble about words when the parliamentary secretary says there were not complaints. I take this to mean there were no representations whatever.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No writing, no correspondence.

The oil industry is usually pretty quick to make its views known, and I am therefore encouraged by the fact that there have been no representations. But with my own knowledge of the oil industry, and particularly of the production end of it, of the supply of the tanks, treaters, separators and the pipe lines, I have a strong reservation in my mind, particularly where a company is just getting established, that a 5 per cent protection is not very much of an incentive, particularly where a person is trying to establish a new industry in competition with established importers who already have their customers, some of whom are in very set lines.
Over the past two years the efforts of the government have been to try and get more and more manufacturing industries in Canada, and that is the reason I am talking about the 5 per cent rate. The 10 per cent rate seemed to be enough of a margin to enable a new manufacturer to have a price advantage, but even that price advantage might not be sufficient in his favour. He may be able to compete on even terms with his United States competitor, but the handiness of local supply and delivery can give him enough to work on. I shall do some checking on this, something I should have done earlier, with regard to some of the newly started firms in my own area.
It seems to me that if there has not been been a complaint received it is because business is good-because there is just now tremendous activity. But this activity only lasts

a while and then they get back to normal, and this is when complaints may arise. I am afraid we are likely to have a lot of complaints as the new field develops to the point where the first rush of business is over.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I think the point made by the hon. member is well taken-that in boom times business is so good that one does not complain about such things as changes in tariffs. But the over-all effect of the changes in these items is in favour of the producer. In order to negotiate them with our tariff partners we had to include three items which were outside the oil field. We had to do this in order to reach agreement.

I should like to refer, for a few moments, to item 683-barytes. This is an important product in my area and its production employs a considerable number of men. I notice that the most favoured nation tariff is being reduced from 25 per cent to 20 per cent and I wonder how this will affect production of this material, particularly in the light of the fact that the market is a very competitive one. Is the recommendation of the tariff board being followed in this respect?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. member was not present earlier. On the matter I raised concerning the tariff on imported aircraft of a class or kind not made in Canada, may I begin by saying that those interested'in aviation in Canada generally, and I am not simply

Customs Tariff
speaking of the air line companies, are very-concerned about the intentions of the department with respect to the imposition of what has amounted to a controversial 15 per cent tariff on aircraft exceeding a gross weight of 2500 pounds but not exceeding 4500 pounds.
The application for the imposition of this tariff was first made by an Ontario aviation company, and I understand it has been under consideration in the department, as well as by the government generally, for some time. I do not believe the government has made any decision as yet. In the absence of such a decision there is a good deal of unrest among aircraft outlets in Canada and, indeed, there has been some speculation in aircraft sales and purchases. I believe it would be in the best interests of the industry as a whole if the parliamentary secretary could now state just what is the policy of the government in this regard and say whether or not the tariff is to be imposed. From the wording of this item no. 440m, it appears as if the tariff will be imposed on and after July 1, 1965. I may be incorrect in this assumption and, if I am, I hope the parliamentary secretary will so inform me.
I know the suggestion has been made to officials of the department that rather than impose a 15 per cent tariff on aircraft of the weight in question, when imported into Canada, there should be an abandonment of the United States tariff now imposed on aircraft of a gross weight above 4500 pounds. This, of course, would result very favourably in this way, that the aircraft industry of Canada would enjoy a freer flow of trade between Canada and the United States, particularly such companies as de Havilland, who sell a good many Beaver aircraft all around the world. The Otter aircraft is another I can think of, and the Caribou is finding growing popularity around the world. If the United States were to drop the tariffs now imposed on that classification of aircraft, rather than Canada imposing its 15 per cent duty on aircraft of between 2,500 and 4,500 pounds gross weight, I think probably the side effects would be a good deal more beneficial to Canada than the result of this tax.
We are in this position, that there is no aircraft manufacturer in Canada today that manufactures aircraft of less than 4,500 pounds gross weight. Most of these are imported from the United States. Cessna Aircraft Corporation provides a good proportion of the market, as does Piper and the Beech-craft Corporation. Now we have one Canadian manufacturer-an enterprising manufacturer, I might say-who is coming along with a five-place aircraft of between 2,500 and 4,500 pounds gross weight. The immediate thought is that in order to give protection to

this growing industry we will put a tariff on such aircraft coming into this country, but I do not think that is a healthy way of encouraging the growth of the aircraft industry in Canada. I will have more to say about that matter if the parliamentary secretary cannot say now that government policy is not to impose this tariff.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to deal with item 440m(l) and 440n(l), which is an extension of the present free entry provision for a year. One of the questions raised by the hon. member was the reduction or removal of both the United States and Canadian tariffs on aircraft. This possibility will be raised at the GATT negotiations;
I can give him this undertaking. As a matter of fact, detailed submissions in this regard are presently being considered by the tariffs and trade committee which was set up by the government in anticipation of the GATT negotiation. This committee is under the chairmanship of Mr. Norman Robertson, with Mr. Hector McKinnon as the vice-chairman. As to the question raised by the hon. member with respect to special types of aircraft, this speculation has arisen from a request to the Department of National Revenue by a firm in Malton, Found Brothers Aviation Ltd., for a change in the made in Canada classification of certain aircraft under item 440m. At present only single engine, fixed wing aircraft for civilian use weighing from 4,500 ot 8,000 pounds are ruled to be of a type or size made in Canada. This provides protection for such aircraft as the Otter and Beaver aircraft manufactured by de Havilland.
Found Brothers have asked that the made in Canada ruling be extended to cover aircraft weighing from 2,500 to 4,500 pounds in order to provide a 15 per cent duty for a new model which they are producing, weighing 2,950 pounds. This request is under review by the Department of National Revenue. If and when any changes are made in the present ruling, they will be issued in the usual way by the Department of National Revenue.
I cannot say that the government policy is so-and-so in this matter, because this is a matter which is under consideration at the present time and a decision has not been made at this point.

Mr. Chairman, can the committee be assured at least to this extent, that there is going to be no imposition of the controversial 15 per cent tariff on aircraft weighing between 2,500 and 4,500 pounds imported into Canada, at least until July 1, 1965? Can the parliamentary secretary give us that assurance?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I do not think I can give that undertaking, Mr. Chairman, because it turns on the decision made on the facts of the case raised by Found Brothers whether or not such aircraft are going to be classified as of a type or size made in Canada. The answer to the second question asked by the hon. member hinges on the answer that I gave to the first question; so really I cannot answer the second question in the affirmative without answering the first one positively, which I did not do.

What I am trying to do there, Mr. Chairman, is end some speculation that has been generated as a result of the indecisiveness of the government in this connection. Here Found Brothers have made an application to the department. This application was made several months ago, and knowledge of it has become quite general throughout the aircraft industry in Canada. Therefore you find dealers in aircraft scurrying to import them from the United States in order to stock them and sell them before what they fear will be the imposition of this 15 per cent duty.
The matter has been before the government long enough now, surely, for them to end this type of speculation and this anxiety within the industry in Canada, simply by saying what is the position. If they cannot say now, "We have decided to impose the 15 per cent tariff", surely the parliamentary secretary could at least rise and say, "We have not yet done so, but it is our intention to bring the matter to a head and announce a decision within the next two or three months", or whatever it might be-perhaps in 60 days.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I should indicate to the hon. member, Mr. Chairman, the difficulty in regard to this particular question. The particular firm, Found Brothers Aviation Ltd., which has raised this question, had until recently only produced two aircraft of this particular size. You then have the Department of National Revenue faced with having to make a decision as to whether or not specific types of aircraft are of a type or size made in Canada when there is a very small production of these aircraft in Canada. This has to be a matter of fact, and I would say one would have to see how these people are going to produce; if their production line is going to go along and they are going to produce quantities of this aircraft. After seeing what is done in this regard, one can make a decision.
As I understand it, only two aircraft have been produced, and one can hardly make a ruling that something has happened based on a very small production such as this. This is the situation we face at the present time.
Customs Tariff
Nevertheless, they have asked the department to consider whether or not this aircraft can be ruled as being of a type or size being made in Canada, and the department will keep looking into this matter and come up with a decision as soon as it is physically possible.

This is the type of answer we have been getting to questions time after time when they have been asked in the house. Here we have speculation that is growing day by day because of the indecisiveness of the government on what seems to be a relatively simple decision to make. I think the parliamentary secretary is looking at the problem from the wrong end of the stick. Instead of saying, "We are not deciding because all we have involved here are two aircraft", he should perhaps be looking at it from our point of view and saying, "We are going to decide not to impose the 15 per cent tariff on this classification of aircraft imported into Canada", because there have been only two produced since Found Brothers went into production, if for no other reason.
But quite apart from that, the parliamentary secretary should consider, too-if my information is correct-the representations that have been made, or the feelings of the management of Beechcraft Corporation, Piper Corporation, Cessna Corporation, de Havilland Corporation. All these Canadian and United States aircraft manufacturers seem to be in accord with the principle of eliminating the tariffs entirely. This undoubtedly would redound to the lasting benefit of the Canadian aviation industry and would encourage the growth of that industry. It is astonishing if, in the face of the representations made by the United States aircraft industry in this particular field of aircraft production, the Canadian government should have any difficulty whatsoever in negotiating the mutual abolition of tariffs on aircraft crossing both ways across the border.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has indicated some indecision. I really do not believe there is any indecision, in that the department holds these aircraft at the present time as not made in Canada. Therefore the only indecision that has arisen is because of a rumour that someone starts, or speculation that someone starts, that we are going to impose a class or kind legislation ruling with regard to this particular type of aircraft. The speculation does not come from within the government; the government's position is firm in this regard. We are standing on the position that they are not at the present time made in Canada. This is our position at this point. As we have said, the government intends to keep looking at this matter as the

Customs Tariff
production of these aircraft increases with this particular firm.
If a point is reached where they can say it is of a class or kind made in Canada perhaps a change in the present ruling will be made. Nevertheless the present ruling is a firm one. There is nothing wishy-washy about it and the government is not hedging in the matter. They simply say that they are not made in Canada, and all the speculation and letters written last month was a result of someone starting a hot rumour about something they did not know too much about.

I really cannot let the parliamentary secretary get away with that. He knows as well as I do that his departmental officials have been corresponding not in any way confidentially with people outside the department in connection with the imposition of the 15 per cent duty. So that when he says that there has been an unfounded or a hot rumour floating around the country about the imposition of a 15 per cent tariff, he is talking through the top of his head, because it is his department itself which received the application from Found Brothers. It was also his department which exchanged correspondence with Found Brothers and others, which has given substance to this consideration, not rumour. The parliamentary secretary said this afternoon that his department is considering the imposition of this duty, so it is not simply a rumour. The speculation which requires to be terminated now is that there is going to be a 15 per cent duty imposed on this classification of aircraft imported into Canada; and so that everybody in the Canadian aviation industry can rest at ease the government should end this speculation which has been generated as a result of its own indecision. The consideration of this matter, as the parliamentary secretary knows-and if he does not know he should-started in his own department back in 1963. It seems that the passage of some eight months is a little too long; that is why I say there has been an indecisiveness displayed on the part of the government in dealing with this matter.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I can answer the hon. member fairly easily. First of all it is not our department at all about which he is talking, but the Department of National Revenue. They consider this matter.
Well, it is your resolution.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Yes, the resolution comes under the Department of Finance. But an application was made to the department to make a class or kind ruling in this particular instance. The department then corresponded openly with people who were going to be involved

in any such ruling, and it is quite necessary that they do this. For example, anybody can manufacture anything for which there is a preferential tariff, if it is of a class or kind made in Canada. An application can be made to have something ruled as a class or kind made in Canada, in which case the department will immediately start correspondence with the people concerned. But this does not mean-
It is not a rumour then, is it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The rumour which I intimated was being spread was that we are going to make a certain kind of ruling in this instance. It has to be considered. Everybody concerned has to be considered, but no class or kind ruling would be made until 10 per cent of the normal market is manufactured in Canada. That is the basis on which a ruling is made. The department will continue, of course, to look into the matter and watch what is being done, which is what they should do. I think that the speculation which was rampant last month arose out of somebody indicating that a change was going to be made.

I did not say it was rampant. I think I should draw the matter to a logical conclusion by saying this. If I can interpret the waffling which the parliamentary secretary has done around this matter, what he is saying in effect is that the government has not yet made up its mind in connection with the imposition of a 15 per cent tariff, despite the fact that it has been under consideration for eight months or more; and that no firm word at all can be given to the Canadian aviation industry at this time. Is that the position which the government is taking?

I rise on a point of order. I submit the argument raised by the hon. member is completely out of order, Mr. Chairman. We are discussing a change to a tariff item in a resolution. Certain tariffs are set up for aircraft of a class or kind made in Canada. The whole subject matter raised by the hon. member opposite concerns a ruling as to whether or not an aircraft is of a class or kind made in Canada. If it is, it falls under a certain tariff item; if it is not it does not. It has nothing to do with the tariff as such, so I feel that the discussion which we have had is completely out of order. We should be discussing only the item in the resolution which concerns the amount of tariff. Whether an item falls in or out of a class or kind made in Canada ruling is a matter for the Department of National Revenue and should not be discussed here.
I might say that I have strong sympathy for the case which the hon. member is trying

to put forward. I do not want to see this tariff imposed, but I think that this is the wrong place to discuss it.

The hon. member may not have been in the chamber when I opened my remarks in connection with this item. The general principle which I put to the parliamentary secretary was that of the abolition of the tariff entirely, both from Canada and from the United States, on classes of aircraft now affected by this particular resolution. Then I went tendentiously into the matter of broadening the class or kind of aircraft which is going to be ruled as of a class or kind made in Canada, and it seemed to me that on that ground I was in order.

Might I just say a few words in respect of the remarks made by the parliamentary secretary. While the hon. member for Yukon says that reports of what the government intend to do may not be widespread, may I say that I have received a great deal of communication, mostly from private aircraft users, potential purchasers, etc. Bearing in mind that this comes into effect on and after July 1, and in view of the fact that the parliamentary secretary can give us no assurance as to when the government can be a little firmer in its attitude in this connection, would the government not consider withdrawing this at this time, and bringing it forward once the industry which caused this application to be made has been more firmly established, or given some indication that they will get 10 per cent of the market. In this way there would be a little more certainty both in the industry and in connection with potential purchasers?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: To withdraw this resolution at this time because the item runs out on July 1 would mean that it would have exactly the opposite effect to what the hon. member wants. It would mean that all aircraft would be subject to 15 per cent tariff coming into Canada.
You could withdraw the 15 per cent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
No, I do not think we should withdraw it. This is a class or kind problem which arises, not just with regard to aircraft but with regard to many other items. The department must of necessity look at these matters on a continuing basis. Its present decision is not waffling. It has made a firm decision that the present ruling is that these aircraft are not of a class or kind made in Canada. That is a firm ruling, as I stated before. Someone has made an application for a change in that ruling with regard to a particular type of aircraft, asking that it be ruled as a
Customs Tariff
class or kind made in Canada. This decision will not be made. One cannot rule it as of a class or kind made in Canada until the producer has obtained 10 per cent of the Canadian market. As far as I am informed, the producer has only produced a very small number of aircraft. One cannot say that the matter is closed forever because the position may change in the relatively near future or in the distant future.
Then can we wind this up with a commitment from the parliamentary secretary that this tariff will not be imposed until the company concerned obtains 10 per cent of the market?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is true in a general way.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED CHANGE OF TERMINOLOGY IN LEGISLATION
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of changing the terminology in the designation "old age" as contained in both the Old Age Assistance Act, being chapter 199 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, and amendments thereto, and the Old Age Security Act, being chapter 200 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, and amendments thereto, to a more worthy designation, so that the aforesaid will be known as the "senior citizens assistance act" and "senior citizens security act" respectively.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in introducing this resolution may I say that I placed the same resolution on the order paper of the house last session but at that time it was not reached for discussion. I have presented it again this session and it now appears as No. 14 on the order paper. I do not intend to speak for long. I hope hon. members in all parts of the house will have something to say on it and will agree with the resolution I have put forward.
I should like to refer to how the matter came to my attention, and perhaps it has come to the attention of other hon. members in a similar way. One day I was speaking to a constituent of mine who is a retired C.N.R. worker and who is far from what might be called old age. He retired from the Canadian National at their retirement age. He is a man who was very active while working with the C.N.R. and has been active later in many community projects.
He suggested that there should be some changes in these acts. He said to me: "I do not feel like I am old. What do you think about this?" I said to him that I had heard the designation "senior citizens" used for a number of years in various parts of the country and I told him that the best and only way I knew to bring this matter to the attention of the government was to bring it forward by way of a notice of motion in the House of Commons.
It has been my experience that many men and women in the group from 65 to 69 who come under the Old Age Assistance Act and in the group 70 and over who come under the Old Age Security Act certainly are not what one would call old. So far as political life is concerned, I must say that in working with

different organization chairmen, other supporters and also constituents of mine in the last few years I have found that those in these two age groups have given me good advice and I have also enjoyed their company. My mind goes back to the days when I was attending college and working in and around the coal mines of my constituency. I recall quite well various people in these age groups with whom I worked. May I say that, although I was a young man at the time, they put me to shame by the amount of work they could do. I noticed that just within the last year or so some of these people celebrated their 60th wedding anniversary, at which time I was able to congratulate them. In my opinion, they are certainly far from old age.
May I point out briefly the history of the two acts involved in this resolution? Some of the social welfare measures which have come to occupy an important position in the Canadian system of social justice may be summed up as follows: first, the original Old Age Pension Act of 1927 provided a maximum pension of $20 per month. The federal contribution at that time was limited to one half the cost. In 1931 the act was amended and the federal share was increased to three quarters of the total cost. The original act was further amended to increase the amount of pension to $25 per month in 1943; to $30 per month in 1947; to $40 per month in 1949-
The Aciing Speaker (Mr. Batten): Order; I hesitate to interrupt the hon. member but I should point out to him that the resolution before us is one to change the terminology of the Old Age Security Act and the Old Age Assistance Act. I suggest to him that a discussion of the amounts of these pensions is not within the terms of this resolution.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with much attention to the interesting speech made by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. MacEwan) and I wish to congratulate him for presenting that motion to change the term "old age".
Last year, Mr. Speaker, I put on the order paper a similar motion bearing no. 30 but the session came to an end before it could be discussed.
That motion, which was put on the order paper at the very beginning of the session, that is on May 17, 1963, read as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of amending the titles of the old age assistance and the old age security acts and deleting the words "old age" from official documents, and substituting therefor a more appropriate designation which will not reflect on the status of recipients of such payments.
Mr. Speaker, I did not suggest then any particular terminology, knowing that such a 
matter could be discussed and that the officials of the department as well as the hon. member would certainly be qualified to make suggestions.
However, I have been pleased to note this year that the hon. member for Pictou had put a similar motion on the order paper. I note that he suggests some terms which obviously in French may not have the same meaning as in English. In English, the legislation is called the "senior citizen's assistance act" which has been translated in French by "Loi sur l'assistance aux citoyens d'age avance." This could evidently lead to a rather interesting debate, to wit if the French translation conveys the idea of the hon. member for Pictou when he refers to "senior citizens".
Now, Mr. Speaker, a discussion to establish whether the French translation well renders the meaning of "senior citizen" in English, would be rather academic in itself. But I entirely agree with the hon. member for Pictou.
On the other hand, when I put that motion on the order paper last year, I stirred up the rage of certain newspapermen. I believe that if the hon. member for Pictou is not yet the butt of their attacks, he will soon be. This proves that everybody cannot share the same opinion.
Last year, on May 25, that is a week after I put this motion on the order paper, a well-known Ottawa paper, the Ottawa Journal, said this in an editorial:

Is old age a disgrace, a shame?

The newspaperman was referring to the term "senior citizen".

Mr. Lachance, a Montreal Liberal, makes it sound as if it were.
He has put on the House of Commons order paper a notice of motion to have the government consider the advisability of amending the titles of the Old Age Assistance and Old Age Security acts and deleting the words "old age" from official documents.
He would substitute "a more appropriate designation which will not reflect on the status of recipients of such payments."
Age is an honourable estate, we wish our friends old age, we associate age with wisdom and we each have the ambition to make a hundred or more.
If not "old age" what then? If Mr. Lachance proposes to change "old age" to "senior citizens" we hope every over-70 sends him a poison letter.

Mr. Speaker, I have no doubt that the hon. member for Pictou will be a butt for the newspapermen, if he has not already been so, following this discussion today.
As I said a while ago-

Which shows that everyone cannot share the same opinion. But I think that when a person reaches about 70 years of age and receives then his old age pension, it is an honour, although some people may get it before.
Some people are inclined to think of the old age pension as a disgrace, a stigma, while in fact it is rather an honour done to our citizens who have acquired the right to be thanked for the services they have rendered to their country.
1 fully agree that we should change the words "old age" and replace them by others which, perhaps, could mean or imply the receipt of a retirement social pension. It is obvious that several other names could be suggested.
I have noticed that in some districts of Montreal, one of whose ridings I have the honour to represent-and I know that this is true also in other regions of the country- one hears about "the golden age". Those are clubs of people who have reached a certain age, and their membership is large. They organize recreational activities for their members. Known as "golden age clubs", they are very popular in Montreal and their members are very happy to belong to them.
We might adopt such a name that would not reflect on people's age. I sincerely admit that it is not very pleasant to get an old age pension and feel it is something to be ashamed of. I am convinced that it is because of our standard of living that life expectancy has increased in Canada and that old age has lost so much of its importance nowadays that a person is old only inasmuch as he feels old.
We all know people who, in spite of the fact that they are well advanced in years, feel young at heart, wish to remain young and have no intention of being considered as older citizens. One is old only if he says he is old and acts accordingly. Some people are old at 20 whereas others feel so well at 80 that they set an example to many much younger persons.
Consequently, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Pictou once more. I feel the wording should be changed but I am not sure whether the words "senior citizens" would be appropriate. The expression "golden age" could surely be used. We could also speak of a "retirement social pension" or of a "national retirement pension". There are other words, but the English expression "old age" and its French equivalent "vieillesse"
Pensions
as in old age pension and "pension de vieillesse" are old-fashioned.
Nowadays, people are not old when they reach a certain age. What would happen if the government suddenly decided tomorrow to grant old age pensions at age 60 as it has often been suggested in the house? Would it mean that people would be old at 60 years of age? And if this process should continue, a day might come when people would receive an old pension at 55 years of age. Would that mean that because they have reached that age they would be in the "old age pension" class?
The old age pension should not be related to a matter of age. It would certainly be beneficial if the terminology relative to social legislation were to be changed, because it is not intended to stigmatize the citizens, but rather to help them and to prove to them the nation's recognition for their good work of the past.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I hope that the newspapermen, or rather the newspaperman who, last year, was good enough to express his opinion on this subject-he was certainly at liberty to do so and I congratulate him-will have changed his mind this year and that he will accept such an excellent suggestion.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is a good idea for us to take a look at the terminology of the two pieces of legislation to which reference is made in the motion now before us. Therefore I join with the hon. member for Lafontaine (Mr. Lachance) in congratulating the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. MacEwan) for inviting us to have this discussion this afternoon.
I must say that there is something to the suggestion that the word "old" and the words "old age" do, sometimes, suggest something unpleasant and if we could find better terminology it would be a good idea. However, I am not completely sold on "senior citizens" as a phrase to take the place of "old age" in this legislation. As the hon. member has just said, if we bring down the retirement age we may be paying old age pensions to people who are not as senior as pensioners are now. None the less I think it would be a good idea for us to look at this. Others may come up with suggestions, and perhaps our friends in the press will not only make comments on what has been said here today but may themselves come up with suggestions. I wonder whether we cannot at least "try on for size" such phrases as "the retirement security act" or "the retired persons act" or "the retired persons pension act".

Pensions
I am interested in the comment made by the last speaker as to finding a word or terminology which can be used easily in both our official languages. That will always have to be considered, but it does strike me that the word "retirement" in some form might fit a little better than the word "senior". In any case, if we can get rid of the word "old", that might be desirable.
I must say that when one talks about a stigma in relation to this legislation, not many people feel that it is so much of a stigma to have the name "old age" applied to their pensions as it is to feel the stigma of the means test in the case of pensions under the Old Age Assistance Act and the inadequacy of the amount in the case of payments under the Old Age Security Act. If we are interested in doing away with a stigma, the thing to do is to make the other kind of improvements in this legislation. I can see already the letters that some of us are going to receive after this debate. We are going to get letters from old age security recipients across Canada who will have noted this debate, and they will say: What are you worrying about the name of the act for, when what we are concerned about is having an adequate pension on which to live in this day and age in the light of the kind of economy we have at the present time? When we are talking about changing the names of this pension legislation we might bear in mind as an ideal getting rid altogether of what we now call the Old Age Assistance Act. I hope the day is not far off when a combination of the Old Age Security Act with its being made available at a lower age, together with the protection of the Canada pension plan, if we are ever to get it on the statute books, will do away with the necessity of any means test on old age pensions for those between the ages of 65 and 70.
Mr. Speaker, you have been very lenient with me. I realize I have got away from terminology. I have been talking about such things as the amount of the pension, the means test and the Canada pension plan. But I do suggest that if we are concerned about a stigma-and that word was used by a previous speaker-we must be concerned not only with the naming of the legislation but with its terms. In other words, as was said by the hon. member who has just spoken, we must be concerned not only with the terminology but with the terms of the legislation. Nevertheless I believe it is a good idea to think about this for a bit this afternoon.

sorry I was not in my own place when I first rose, Mr. Speaker. I do not wish to add very much to the discussion, but simply to say that I join with previous speakers who have

discussed the noble enterprise of changing the names of the acts referred to. I agree there is something depressing about the names now used-"old age assistance", "old age pensions", and so on.

I think that at the present time a great deal of money is needed to run these separate programs. We have a whole hierarchy of systems. If there were an over-all social security plan for Canada it would represent one answer to the problem raised by the hon. member for Pictou, who wants to change the names of these acts.

With the greatest respect, Mr. Speaker, I think we are dealing here with a matter that is on a twofold plane. We are dealing, first, with the renaming of statutes, and second we are dealing with the subject of old age. Therefore with respect I would submit that remarks referable to either of these basic ingredients of the hon. gentleman's resolution are pertinent and relevant and I trust will be of some help to hon. members in determining their respective choices in regard to the resolution. Again, on the question of renaming the acts, if it would be of some help to this house I might suggest that the Income Tax Act be renamed something along these lines, "An act for the purpose of removing coin of the realm from the pockets of those who have to those who have not". I feel this would be the type of concise and appropriate name which surely would not offend the great majority of our people. I am sure most hon. members of this house, from all I have heard since I have been here, receive little support from those who have great wealth, those from whom it would be removed; so the name should bear the approval of all hon. members as well as all citizens.
With respect, Mr. Speaker, I think when we are speaking about names, whether names have a particular connotation, whether a name is particularly offensive, or whether a certain name is better than another, it would not be right, proper or fitting if we based our deliberations on that score without considering the best words ever spoken with regard to the question of what's in a name. I quote from Romeo and Juliet, act 2, scene 2, line 40:
O be some other name! What's Montague?
It is nor hand, nor foot, nor arm, nor face.
Nor any part belonging to a man.
What's in a name? That which we call a rose
By any other name would smell as sweet.
I offer these words of wisdom to the hon. member for Pictou and suggest that the gist of the old age pension bill and the Old Age Assistance Act is very much more what has been brought to our attention by hon. members, and certainly by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), namely what is in the bill itself. How much are these people receiving, and are they getting it with a minimum of embarrassment and without a means test? I believe the old age pension by any other name would smell just as sweet if we could see to it that that pension, accompanied with the Canada pension plan which is shortly to be before the house, provides the older people of this country with the wherewithal whereby they may live out their senior years in dignity and without want. This, surely, is the important matter, not the name of the bill itself.
In the not too distant future we hope to be doing some serious thinking in regard to the Canada pension plan, which will indeed fit in with the present legislation as it now exists. If the hon. member feels there is some very great national benefit in his resolution he might raise the matter at such time, either by way of amendment in committee when discussing the proposed measure, or in some other way.
There is one other aspect to the hon. member's desire to change this name which troubles me. This is the inference that there is something disreputable or unworthy or something we should hide in the very words "old age". I submit to the house that there is nothing unworthy or to be ashamed of about this expression, or which should be hidden under a basket some place. In this regard the legislation which is being brought in, as the hon. member who presented this bill has pointed out over the years, has certainly recognized that old age is a time of dignity worthy of security and well-being. In this connection I think the writers through the ages have recognized the worth of old age. It is not a time for despair. No person should be looked down upon because he is old. I think George Bernard Shaw put it as well as any of us could when he stated something along these lines-that until you are 60 you really have not learned enough to be of much use to anyone; and until you are 80 you have not had enough practice in application to put that knowledge you have acquired to use. I think Victor Hugo put it very well when he said:

When grace is joined with wrinkles it is adorable. There is an unspeakable dawn in a happy old age.
I should like to close my remarks on this delightful and worth-while subject by leaving with the house the thought that I do not think we should do anything here to discredit old age. I do not think there is anything more attractive in the words "senior citizen" than there is in the words "old age". Old age means that a person has given a great many years to this country, to bringing up his family, to paying his taxes, and to earning that very assistance which is paid to him, not by way of any handout from a government or from parliament, but by reason of his playing his part as a citizen of this country and earning whatever emoluments we pay him.
