Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. MacEwan) on his very generous motives for introducing this motion in the house.
Mr. Speaker, I did not expect to speak on that motion but in any case, I should like to quote from it. It reads as follows:
That in the opinion of the house, the government should consider the advisability of changing the terminology in the designation "old age"-
So, the point is to change the designation "old age" for the designation "senior citizen". Any dictionary will give you, as definition of old age, the following:
The advanced years in human life.
So, I understand that this discussion is simply an empty battle of words which does not contribute much to the promotion of public business.
Pensions
Mr. Speaker, if I may be out of order for only 30 seconds, I should like to say that I deeply regret that because of our present system of procedure, parliament has to discuss during a whole hour a simple matter of terminology when there are problems of extreme importance facing the country.
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene) put it so well, this motion is only an attempt to find euphemisms, designations to alleviate other designations meaning the same thing.
As a matter of fact, in the phrase old age, there is absolutely nothing reflecting upon a state of life which most people are to know some day.
As a matter of fact, there are two stages in life: birth and death. The main steps between those two stages are childhood, the teen-age period, middle age and old age. Consequently, I fail to see the usefulness of dealing indefinitely with a mere question of terminology.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, if we were going to deal with the terminology of each of our laws, we would get nowhere, and we would get lost in useless talking, without achieving anything.
Let us talk about the word "pension". Is it necessary to insist on that word and say that the fact that a person receives a pension establishes a certain analogy between the words pensioner and parasite? Should we not change the word "pensioner" in order that the person who receives a pension from the government will not be compared to a parasite?
When we talk about the pension to veterans, do we mean that veterans who receive pensions refuse now to fight?
When we speak of unemployment insurance, do we not throw discredit on the unemployed by considering him as a loafer?
Again, would it be necessary to change the terminology of all those acts and say that the unemployed is a loafer, a parasite, that it is an insult to call him "unemployed"?
There is in Quebec a pension for unmarried women. But what an insult, Mr. Speaker, to think that a woman has to stay unmarried. Again, would it not be better to change the terminology of that act? That is an insult to the charm and attractiveness of that sex which ought not to be called the weaker one, because, on the contrary, it exerts a far greater power than one would imagine.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, there has been too much discussion, and that is why I

want to return to my seat as quickly as possible. In my opinion, we have spent too much time debating a subject which, granted, shows the best of intentions on the part of the hon. member for Pictou, who wants to bring in a new expression in the hope of improving a situation which, to his way of thinking, is such as to put older people in a position of inferiority.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that the proper meaning of a term or expression should not be confused with the disparaging intonation it is sometimes given. As a matter of fact, one often calls somebody "old man" or "young man". It may be injurious in both cases but it is only a matter of intonation and not of semantics or real meaning of the word.
In fact, what would the reaction of the hon. member for Pictou be if I were to tell him one day that he is not old enough to be a senator? Lmagine if he would like then to be considered as an old man.
If I told him that he is too young to be a minister, then the word "young" could be disparaging simply because of the manner in which it is spoken.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I agree with the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene) that if we are to consider every act in order to see what term or word could be changed, parliament would waste its time, like it did tonight, whereas if the procedure were amended, we could look into far more important situations likely to prove beneficial to all the people.
